background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, as you heard from the small business owners, Obamacare is not working for people that are on the individual health insurance market. We've seen here in Arizona prices going up over 100% year to year. It's those people who are starting their own business, retiring early, in between jobs, going to schools. This is 7% of how people get insurance that has just collapsed under Obamacare. Only 14 of our 15 counties in Arizona had only one choice last year. And they're often, the costs are way too high or the networks are too small. And people were discovering that just because they have health insurance, they don't have health care. So we need a different model. We must protect people with pre-existing conditions. They cannot be denied coverage. Do not believe the lies of the attack ads on TV. I voted for, I fought for, and I advocated to make sure that insurance companies cannot deny anybody with pre-existing conditions. This touches every single family. We all know somebody or everyone themselves. It has some sort of... You know, someone they love who either is a cancer survivor or they just got the phone call with a diagnosis or they've got asthma or diabetes. So we have to make sure that they're protected. But we also need more innovation and at the state level so that we can have a robust individual health insurance market where there's competition, where there's choices, where people can shop around and pick the insurance that works for them and their families. And someone can start a small business and not be afraid that they're not covered like we heard the stories of in the roundtable today. So there is a better way to do this and the Affordable Care Act is hurting especially this group of people in this individual health insurance market. Small businesses. Small businesses and the people on the individual market. Over 60% of people get their health insurance from their employer when you add in Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA. We're talking this other, this group that's stuck in the middle is this 7%. And think about it, Obamacare was taxes, penalties, mandates, robbing Medicare by $700 billion. All to try and address this issue, but it's failed, specifically this group of people. So we got to move towards something where the states have more opportunities to have innovation, where restaurant owners can work together as an association and they can pool together and get insurance maybe together. Small business owners can pool together and have options to shop around for insurance, where you can compete across state lines, where there's options for people to, you know, young people to shop around and get insurance. That meets their needs that they can afford when they're getting out of school. And so these are the approaches that we need to work more towards more choice, more competition, while also guaranteeing protection for people with pre-existing conditions.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: And you're still looking for ways to, as Obamacare, strive to with the mandate.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Yeah.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: have a large enough pool that it covers the healthy people help cover the sick people.

ground_truth: Well, exactly. So the individual mandate was the Democrats way to do that. We believe more in freedom and choice, but we want to make sure people do get coverage and incentivize continuous coverage. So what we had was tax credit. So people can have pre-tax dollars just like businesses, and then they can shop around. What we're doing right now, the administration is doing, is creating opportunities for these association health plans. Again, a small business maybe can't compete and get insurance for their employers, but maybe the Arizona Association for whatever business they're in can do that with them, and they can all work together and have some strength. We also are trying to expand health savings accounts so people can save pre-tax dollars, pay for their premiums, pay for their deductibles, pay for over-the-counter medication, which Obamacare doesn't allow. These things will all allow people to be able to have more choices, and then we've got to bring down the cost of health care overall. This conversation so far has been the cost of health insurance, which is unattainable for so many people. I mean, think about the people with pre-existing conditions. They had pre-existing conditions last year who paid a penalty instead of getting health insurance. They don't have access to health insurance. So we've got to make sure that they can get the insurance they need, they can get the prescriptions that they and their families need at an affordable price, and you have a healthy insurance market that has young and old, sick and healthy, and that actually keeps the prices lower.
bio: Martha Elizabeth McSally (born March 22, 1966) is an American politician and former military pilot who served as a United States Senator for Arizona from 2019 to 2020. A Republican, she served as the U.S. Representative for Arizona's 2nd congressional district from 2015 to 2019. McSally served in the United States Air Force from 1988 to 2010, achieving the rank of Colonel. She is the first U.S. woman to fly in combat and also the first to command a fighter squadron. The speaker's MBTI type is ESTJ

background.text: When you talk about going across state lines to improve the competition,

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: Right now, the principal watchdogs on the insurance industry are the state insurance commissioners. Right. Who would take on that role if you're crossing state lines? So, again...

ground_truth: We prefer that a lot of this innovation gets worked at the state level, but something like the association health plans, the administration is working on options so that you can, again, as a restaurant association between states, you could work together and maybe have a bigger pool that you're competing for health insurance. This actually happens already with larger business that are multi-state businesses, that they have reciprocal agreements. So there's a way to do that. But we'd prefer not a federal one-size-fits-all robbing Medicare of $700 billion, a trillion dollars in taxes, all for basically a failing system that's unattainable for people to afford their health insurance right now. Let's take a fresh look. Let's provide choices for people. Let's allow the states to innovate. Let's use the taxpayer resources that are being invested in a way that invests in those that have the most complex health care issues, provide wraparound services to them, allow the states to use the stability fund that we created in our legislation. For them to bring premiums down, bring costs down, and have more choices for people, that's a better model.

background.text: Well, first of all, I'm not trying to change Social Security and Medicare, so don't believe those attack ads. Those who have worked their whole lives and they are at and near retirement, they have been planning on Social Security and Medicare, and we need to make sure that we keep those promises. Now, in 2026, Medicare is not going to be solvent, and in 2034, Social Security won't be. So we have to work in a bipartisan way in order to strengthen those programs for the following generations. So those lies on TV are absolutely not true. Those are just fear tactics related to people who don't have anything else to run on. But I really do believe if you look at what's happening with our economy right now, we have more people working because we cut taxes, we roll back regulations, there's more people paying payroll taxes. That right there is actually making these two programs more solvent because we have more people paying into it. But we've got to strengthen and sustain these programs for future generations. Medicare Advantage is another one that's very popular. Medicare Advantage is another one that's very popular. Medicare Advantage is another one that's very popular in [state]. We have a lot of seniors who like to look for different Medicare Advantage programs, and they really do a lot of good work. So the last administration was trying to cut Medicare Advantage, and I helped lead the fight to make sure that stopped from happening. So we need to preserve that as well.

ground_truth: The [state] economy is going strong. My opponent did not vote to cut your taxes. I voted to cut your taxes. We're rolling back regulations. We're providing small businesses the opportunity to grow and hire more people, and we're seeing that right here in [state]. There's also initiatives at the state level that the governor has had to bring businesses here and take advantage of a great environment that's welcoming to companies that want to bring their workers and their families here, and that's fantastic. On our part at the federal level, I'm also focusing on preserving our national security facilities like [military base 1] and [military base 2]. They have a really important economic impact, and you know I've been leading the charge to keep the A-10 flying, the EC-130s, and all the important missions here at [military base 1] and [military base 2]. Also, infrastructure is another important element. The highway bill, we've got some big wins in that. The [regional] Corridor is another one that can be game-changing that's got some federal influence there. I got that in the highway bill. And then [country] is our top trading partner, so the modernization of [trade agreement] is a win-win-win for America, [country], and Canada, but especially for [state] businesses. background.speaker: [target]
background.text: We have to secure the border. I'm one of only nine members of Congress right now that represents the southern border. And as a freshman, I was appointed the chair of the Border Security Subcommittee, never given to a freshman before, never given to anyone from Arizona. So I've been in that leadership position, fighting to secure the border, working with this administration. I represent fifth generation ranchers that are down on the border, that are dealing with four strands of barbed wire is all that demarks the international boundary. They've got cartels trafficking drugs through their ranches. They've got human trafficking happening as well. And then we have individuals, because of the loopholes in our laws, that are realizing that they're going to be let go if they just say a few words or if they show up with a kid. And so we have to close these loopholes. We have to secure the border. That's going to take investing in infrastructure. It means investing in the border wall, investing in access roads and technology, the fixed towers, the mobile towers, the sensors, the manned and unmanned aircraft, border patrol agents. I mean, my bill, I added 5,000 border patrol agents, $38 billion invested in border security for all the things I just mentioned. And the access roads are a really big deal. For some of the ranchers, sometimes it takes an hour and a half to get down there, so it's tough for border patrol to be able to patrol down there. And we need intelligence-driven operations so that they can go after the cartels and their money and their leadership, but also then detect and interdict the illegal activity where it happens. This is really crucial for Arizona. And my bill, actually close these loopholes and provide the resources to secure the border. Unfortunately, my opponent didn't vote for it.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: Is a wall part of this? Is a wall the answer? Part of the answer?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Yeah, absolutely a wall is part of it. Look, the Secure Fence Act was passed in 2005, amended in 2006, mandating 700 miles of a double-layer wall on the border. You know, Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton and Chuck Schumer and Joe Biden all voted for it. They knew that a barrier was an important part of border security back then. This has gotten so ridiculous in the way people even think about it. But if you talk to the ranchers down at the border where they had no barrier before and now they have the 18-foot steel ballard fencing where they maybe used to have nothing, it's more of the, I mean, they have fencing in other areas, but it creates what they call impedance and denial where the cartels have a problem they have to solve. Now, given time, without monitoring it, they'll figure it out. They'll go over it, through it, or under it. But at least it creates that barrier that they have to try and figure out how to get around. And then if you put the agents and the censors down there while they're having to try and figure that out, then it gives us time to be able to interdict that activity. So Jim Chilton's ranch is a perfect example. It's west of Nogales, and that's the one I'm talking about. It's got miles of border that all there is is four lines of chicken wire across. And the cartels, he's got cameras set up, and he sees these drug mules that are just continuously trafficking through his ranch. He wants a barrier down there. He wants a border rule. In areas of the Rio Grande Valley where there's river, obviously, you need more riverine boats. You need more border patrols. You need more border patrol agents monitoring and more censors. In some places, you need a levee system that helps with flood control and creates a barrier. So sector by sector, from the bottom up, that you need the sector chiefs to be able to tell, you know, what do they need to secure that part of the sector. So they have situational awareness and operational control of the border. And in many places, it does include a border wall.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: Now, when people show up with kids, is there a better way to vet them out and figure out which ones are there as a pretense and which ones really are sincerely seeking asylum as a family?

ground_truth: So there's a couple things. The cartels know that because of a loophole in what's called the Flores Agreement, it's a settlement that basically says we can't detain children more than 20 days. They know that anyone who shows up and crosses the border illegally with a kid, we can't detain them. And we're seeing this right now. I've been on the phone all weekend with the mayor of Yuma, totally concerned that they're going to have hundreds of people just released into their community. Now, the good news is they didn't get released into the Yuma community, but they are being released everywhere else now because the cartels know that, hey, we just make sure we're going to have people pay us, show up with a kid, cross illegally, and they're going to be released. They'll be given a court date in the future. They don't have enough ankle monitors, and many of them just don't show up. Others are showing up through the ports of entry, and they've been trained by the cartels. All you have to say is, I have a credible fear, and they start them through the asylum process. Look, we have an important and compelling... We have a compassionate asylum system in order to protect people that are fearing for their lives and oppression by their own governments, but it's being taken advantage of right now. And the people who have legitimate asylum claims are being lost in the sea of those who are now taking advantage of the system. So every single day, we're just having people show up, say the right words, show up with a kid, disappear into the interior of the United States, never to show up for their court date. That doesn't make any sense. That's not compassionate for the people who are filing asylum, who are taking years now to have their case made. So my bill closes those loopholes, allows a swifter process of adjudication for asylum claims, and allows us to enforce the law while keeping families together. And that's the way we need to move forward.
